title: A new neighbour
explanation: Last week a new family moved into the flat next to mine. The mother is called Sara and she works at a hospital. Her son Omar is eight years old and he plays football every afternoon. Yesterday Sara knocked on my door and gave me a cake. I made tea and we talked for an hour. I think we will be good friends.
examples: move into: to start living in a new home
flat: a set of rooms to live in, inside a larger building
knock: to hit a door gently so people know you are there

title: The long commute
explanation: Daniel lives forty kilometres from his office. Every morning he takes a train and then a bus, which takes almost two hours. At first he found the journey exhausting, but he soon discovered that it was the only quiet time in his day. He now uses it to read books and learn languages. Although he would prefer a shorter trip, he admits that the commute has made him more patient.
examples: discover: to find or learn something for the first time

exercises.prompt: What does Daniel use the commute for?
exercises.explain: He reads books and learns languages.

exercises.prompt: What has the commute taught him?
exercises.explain: It has made him more patient.

title: The attention economy
explanation: Many free apps earn money by capturing our attention and selling it to advertisers. The longer users stay on a platform, the more profit it makes, so designers add features such as endless scrolling and constant notifications. Critics argue that these techniques exploit natural psychological habits. Supporters reply that users remain free to leave at any time. The debate raises a broader question: who is responsible for protecting attention, the companies or the individuals?
examples: exploit: to use something unfairly for your own benefit
notification: a message that appears to tell you something new

exercises.prompt: How do many free apps earn money?
options: By selling users' attention to advertisers
exercises.explain: They capture attention and sell it to advertisers.

exercises.prompt: What do critics say about these techniques?
options: They are illegal in all countries
exercises.explain: Critics argue they exploit natural psychological habits.

exercises.prompt: Supporters say users are free to ... at any time. (one word)
exercises.explain: Users remain free to leave at any time.

title: Rethinking the city
explanation: For decades, urban planners prioritised the car, widening roads and relegating pedestrians to narrow pavements. Yet cities that have reclaimed street space for cycling and public transport report cleaner air and livelier neighbourhoods. Sceptics caution that such schemes can displace lower-income residents when rising property values follow improvements. Consequently, the most thoughtful proposals pair infrastructure with affordable housing, so that the benefits of renewal are widely shared rather than concentrated.
examples: relegate: to move to a less important position
displace: to force people to leave their home
concentrated: gathered in one place or group

exercises.prompt: What did planners prioritise for decades?

exercises.explain: Rising property values can displace lower-income residents.

exercises.prompt: What do thoughtful proposals combine infrastructure with?
exercises.explain: They pair it with affordable housing.

title: The limits of translation
explanation: Translators often speak of fidelity and fluency as though they were opposing virtues: the former demands loyalty to the source text, the latter to the reader. Yet this antithesis is arguably too neat. A rendering that preserves every word may betray the spirit of the original, whereas one that smooths away strangeness may erase precisely what made the work distinctive. The accomplished translator, therefore, negotiates rather than resolves this tension, accepting that some loss is inevitable and that the choice of what to sacrifice is itself an interpretive act.
examples: antithesis: a direct contrast between two ideas
inevitable: certain to happen and impossible to avoid

exercises.explain: Fidelity demands loyalty to the source text.

exercises.prompt: What may a word-for-word rendering do?
options: Betray the spirit of the original
exercises.explain: It may betray the spirit of the original.

exercises.prompt: The translator ... the tension rather than resolving it. (one word)
exercises.explain: The accomplished translator negotiates rather than resolves.
